Lesson Overview: Evidence-Based Craft Reasoning

Lesson Focus

Primary: MLA.CW.WR.08 — support craft claims and revision decisions with precise evidence and reasoning.

Supporting: MLA.CW.WR.09 — analyze craft models; MLA.CW.COM.02 — evaluate and use feedback through reasoned decisions. A peer is not required for this lesson; supplied reader comments let you practice evaluating feedback independently.

What You Will Learn

  • Build a claim–evidence–warrant chain that explains how a choice works.
  • Check relevance, sufficiency, and representativeness instead of collecting quotations.
  • Address counterevidence and qualify claims about reader effects.
  • Test a focused revision, explain its trade-off, and define a useful success check.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 6 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task

Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.

TermMeaningExample
craft claimA focused, arguable statement about how a writer’s choice contributes to an effect.The repeated pauses create a craft claim about the narrator’s hesitation.
evidenceExact language, a recurring pattern, or a structural feature that a reader can verify in the text.Three clipped sentences provide evidence of a rushed pace.
warrantThe reasoning that explains how and why the evidence supports the claim.The warrant explains that the fragments imitate interrupted thought.
relevanceHow directly evidence addresses the particular claim being made.A description of sentence length is relevant to a claim about pacing.
sufficiencyWhether the amount and range of evidence justify the scope of the claim.One example may be insufficient for a claim about the entire story.
representativenessHow fairly selected evidence reflects the passage or the specific portion named in the claim.Evidence from the opening and ending better represents the whole passage.
counterevidenceA detail or pattern that challenges, limits, or complicates a claim.A calm final sentence challenges the claim that the tone is entirely frantic.
qualificationLanguage that narrows a claim to match the strength and limits of its evidence.The phrase “in this scene” qualifies a claim that would otherwise be too broad.
causal claimA statement that a choice produces or contributes to an effect; comparison can support it but does not prove every reader will respond alike.The delayed reveal contributes to the reader’s surprise.
revision rationaleAn evidence-based explanation of a change, its intended effect, its trade-off, and how its success will be checked.The writer explains why a revised ending improves tension but reduces ambiguity.

Drag and Drop — Use the Reasoning Vocabulary

Match each term to what a writer or reader is doing. Drag a word, or click it and then its destination. Select Check, read the feedback, and Retry as needed. This is optional, ungraded practice and does not block progress.

See the Difference

EvidenceWarrantQualified claim
“She finished the sentence but left the envelope unsealed.”The contrast between a finished sentence and unfinished closure separates resumed work from a resolved decision.The ending suggests partial progress while leaving the next action open.

Pause and Try

A response quotes three lines and says, “This proves the writing is good.” What is missing?

Pause: say or jot your reasoning before opening the explanation. This is optional, ungraded practice—not a submission.

Check your thinking

A focused craft claim and a warrant. Three quotations are not automatically sufficient or representative. Explain the exact choice, how it contributes to an effect, and any detail that limits the claim.

Reference Glossary — Understand, Do Not Copy

Syntax: the arrangement of words and clauses. Finite verb: a verb showing tense, such as “clicked.” A fragment lacks a complete independent clause; a short sentence is not automatically a fragment. Mechanism: how a choice works. Trade-off: what a change gains and may lose. Success criterion: a specific sign used to judge whether a goal was met. Coincidence: events occurring together without an established causal connection.

Lesson: From Evidence to a Defensible Revision

Start with a Question You Can Test

When I read a draft, I do not begin with “This is good.” I ask: What is the writing trying to help me notice or anticipate? Then I find the exact choice doing that work. Today you will move from noticing to explaining, and from explaining to a revision you can defend.

Our running draft: “The latch clicked. June stopped writing. Footsteps crossed the hall, then faded. She finished the sentence but left the envelope unsealed.” A latch fastens a door; an unsealed envelope is not closed securely.

Step 1 — Separate Intention from Evidence

I might propose an intended effect of interrupted concentration with unresolved hesitation. That is a working goal, not a fact about the author’s mind. The text gives observable actions; my interpretation must answer to them.

Focused claim: The interruption followed by incomplete closure suggests that June resumes her task without fully resolving her hesitation. This is more useful than “The scene is tense” because it names a pattern and its possible function.

Step 2 — Build the Chain Visually

PartAskRunning example
ClaimWhat choice contributes to what effect?Interruption and incomplete closure suggest unresolved hesitation.
EvidenceWhich exact words and pattern support it?“stopped writing” is followed by “finished the sentence” but “left the envelope unsealed.”
WarrantHow does that relationship guide interpretation?Stopping interrupts progress; finishing restores some progress, while the unsealed envelope leaves the next action incomplete.
LimitWhat remains uncertain?The text does not establish fear, the visitor’s identity, or why she leaves it unsealed.

Pause and Try

Which is a warrant: “The passage says unsealed,” or “The unfinished closure keeps sending unresolved even though the writing resumes”?

Pause: say or jot your reasoning before opening the explanation. This is optional, ungraded practice—not a submission.

Check your thinking

The second explains the relationship between completion and incompletion. The first only repeats evidence. A warrant must do reasoning work; it cannot just rename the quotation.

Step 3 — Test Evidence Quality

Do not ask only, “Did I find a quote?” Ask whether your evidence could persuade someone who does not already agree with you.

TestUseful checkCommon error
RelevanceDoes it address my exact claim?Using a wall color to prove hesitation without explaining a connection.
SufficiencyHave I supported the full scope?Using one pause to call an entire scene motionless.
RepresentativenessHave I included important exceptions?Ignoring “finished the sentence” to claim she never resumes.
PrecisionCan another reader locate it?Inventing “her trembling hands” when the text never says it.

A narrow claim about one sentence may need only that sentence. A claim about the whole scene needs a fair view of its pattern. More quotations are not automatically better evidence.

Pause and Choose: Test the Full Evidence Chain

Draft: “The latch clicked. June stopped writing. Footsteps crossed the hall, then faded. She finished the sentence but left the envelope unsealed.”

Which interpretation represents the complete pattern instead of relying on one quotation?

A. June never resumes writing; “stopped writing” proves that the whole scene is paralysis.
Not the best interpretation. Although it quotes the draft, it ignores the counterevidence that June finishes the sentence. One accurate quotation cannot support a claim that misrepresents the rest of the scene.
B. June briefly stops, then resumes, but the unsealed envelope leaves the next action unresolved.
✓ Correct—representative reasoning. This response accounts for interruption, resumed writing, and incomplete closure. It explains the pattern while preserving the unknown motive.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Step 4 — Qualify Instead of Defending an Overstatement

My first thought might be “Every short sentence speeds the scene.” I test it: “June stopped writing” describes a pause. A short sentence can isolate a halt as well as a quick action. Sentence length, punctuation, action, and context work together.

Better: “The brief opening sentences separate the sound and June’s reaction into distinct beats; the later sentence combines renewed progress with an unfinished action.” This describes the mechanism without promising one universal reading speed.

Grammar check: “The latch clicked” has a subject and finite verb and is a complete sentence. “A click at the latch” has no finite verb and is a fragment. Do not call every short sentence a fragment.

Pause and Try

Repair “The entire scene stops because June stops writing.” Use one detail that limits the claim.

Pause: say or jot your reasoning before opening the explanation. This is optional, ungraded practice—not a submission.

Check your thinking

June pauses after the click but later finishes her sentence. A fair claim is that the interruption briefly halts her work while the unsealed envelope leaves the larger decision unresolved. The later action limits “entire.”

Pause and Choose: Qualify the Effect

Sentence: “June stopped writing.”

Which claim accurately connects sentence length, action, and context?

A. Every short sentence speeds the reader through the action.
Overgeneralized. The sentence is short, but its action is a stop. Short units can isolate and emphasize a pause; their effect depends on the words, punctuation, and surrounding passage.
B. The brief sentence isolates June’s halted action, making the interruption noticeable before the scene resumes.
✓ Correct—well qualified. This answer names the arrangement, the actual action, and its local effect without claiming that every reader or every short sentence behaves identically.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Step 5 — Change One Feature, Then Compare

Goal: make the interruption more noticeable without naming June’s motive.

Original: “The latch clicked. June stopped writing.”

Test version: “The latch clicked, and June stopped writing.”

The words and events stay the same; the full stop becomes a conjunction. The original separates sound and response into distinct beats. The combined version links them more smoothly. I would keep the original for a sharper interruption, but I cannot claim the punctuation makes every reader feel fear.

Trade-off: separate beats can emphasize interruption but may feel too choppy if repeated everywhere. Compare the change in the surrounding scene, not in isolation.

Step 6 — Evaluate Feedback with a Success Check

Supplied reader comment: “Tell us who is in the hall.” First ask what difficulty the reader reports. Are they confused about who acts, or curious about an intentionally unknown visitor? Those are different problems.

For our goal, I would keep the visitor unknown but ensure that June’s actions remain clear. I would ask a reader: “What interrupts June, what does she resume, and what remains unfinished?” If the reader can answer those questions, the scene can be clear without a fully explained motive.

A predicted effect is not collected reader evidence. Unless someone actually responds, say “I would check” or “I predict,” not “readers proved.”

Use This Reasoning Frame

The choice ___ may contribute to ___. The details ___ and ___ show ___. They support my claim because ___. However, ___ limits the claim. Changing ___ to ___ would likely ___, with the trade-off ___. I would check success by asking ___.

Use the frame to organize thought, not to add unnecessary sentences. Precise explanation matters more than filling every blank mechanically.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 6 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Evidence-Based Decisions

Watch a Writer Think, Test, and Decide

Each example shows the complete draft, an initial claim, exact evidence, a warrant, a challenge, and a visible revision comparison. Notice that I sometimes repair the claim rather than rewrite the scene. Better reasoning does not always require more words.

Example 1 — Test a Pacing Claim

Original: “The elevator stopped. The lights blinked. A cable struck the shaft, once, then again. Mara counted to five before she breathed.” The shaft is the vertical space in which the elevator travels.

1. Set a goal: suggest danger interrupted by Mara’s attempt at control.

2. Name the evidence accurately: “The elevator stopped” and “The lights blinked” are short complete sentences, not fragments. “Once, then again” spaces the impacts; “counted to five” names deliberate delay.

3. State a warrant: separate sentence boundaries present mechanical failures as distinct beats. The counting shifts attention from external events to Mara regulating her response. This may create alternating shock and delay, not uniform speed.

4. Test the first claim: “The fragments make everything fast” fails twice: the grammar label is wrong, and counting is counterevidence to “everything fast.” I narrow the claim before revising.

5. Compare an actual alternative: “The elevator stopped, and the lights blinked. A cable struck the shaft, once, then again. Mara counted to five before she breathed.”

6. Decide: Only the first boundary changes. The combined version links the failures more smoothly; the original isolates them. I would retain the original for distinct shocks, while acknowledging that some readers may experience its stops as slower. The trade-off is a more segmented rhythm.

Success check: Ask where a reader notices separate failures and where the scene pauses. Do not ask the leading question “Wasn’t the original scarier?”

Pause and Choose: A or B

Why is “The lights blinked” not a fragment? What evidence prevents “uniformly fast” from being a fair claim?

Pause: say or jot your reasoning before opening the explanation. This is optional, ungraded practice—not a submission.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which response gives the stronger evidence-to-reasoning explanation? Choose before opening either response.

A. “The lights” is the subject and “blinked” is a finite verb, so the sentence is complete. The repeated impacts spaced by “once, then again” and Mara’s counting introduce delays. Accurate terminology and representative evidence both matter.
Stronger response. This answer uses specific evidence, explains the reasoning, and connects the choice to the purpose of the model.
B. This response is stronger because it sounds more creative and includes more detail.
Weaker response. This claim is vague. It does not identify exact evidence, explain a reader effect, or connect the choice to the writer’s purpose.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Revise the Claim Before Revising the Symbol

Original: “Theo carried the cracked compass through three cities. At the border, he traded it for bread without looking back.” A compass indicates direction; a border separates places or territories.

1. Initial claim: “The compass proves permanent attachment to home.” That sounds literary, but where does the text identify home? It does not.

2. Evidence: carrying it through three cities suggests continued usefulness or value. Trading it for bread shows a changed priority. “Without looking back” complicates a claim of visibly reluctant release.

3. Warrant: duration establishes that the object has stayed with Theo; exchanging it for food sets a limit on keeping it. Emotional attachment is possible, but practical usefulness is a plausible alternative.

4. Qualified claim: “The retained object becomes exchangeable when an immediate need takes priority.” This fits both sentences without inventing the compass’s origin or Theo’s feelings.

5. Test a revision for a chosen goal: Suppose I want to make the cost of parting more visible. Original: “At the border, he traded it for bread without looking back.” Revision: “At the border, he traded it for bread, then traced the empty circle it had worn into his pocket.”

6. Compare and decide: The new tactile action draws attention to absence after the exchange. I would use it for lingering awareness; the trade-off is losing the original’s brisk departure. It still does not identify home or prove regret.

Success check: Ask what the final action makes a reader notice after the trade. If the goal were decisive release instead, the original might serve it better.

Pause and Choose: A or B

A reader says, “The compass is from his mother.” Can adding “perhaps” make that a supported interpretation?

Pause: say or jot your reasoning before opening the explanation. This is optional, ungraded practice—not a submission.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which response gives the stronger evidence-to-reasoning explanation? Choose before opening either response.

A. This response is stronger because it sounds more creative and includes more detail.
Weaker response. This claim is vague. It does not identify exact evidence, explain a reader effect, or connect the choice to the writer’s purpose.
B. Not by itself. The passage gives no family origin. Qualification adjusts certainty; it cannot supply missing evidence. Discuss the object’s demonstrated retention and exchange, or add new story evidence if the writer deliberately wants a family connection.
Stronger response. This answer uses specific evidence, explains the reasoning, and connects the choice to the purpose of the model.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 3 — Evaluate Feedback without Treating It as a Vote

Original: “The courtroom emptied. Inez stacked every paper except the unsigned statement, which she folded into her sleeve.” A bailiff is a courtroom officer; an unsigned statement lacks a signature.

Supplied feedback: Reader A infers concealment. Reader B notices that the paper is important but is unsure about secrecy. These are two observations about reader response, not proof of how all readers react.

1. Set a goal: make concealment more noticeable while leaving its motive open.

2. Locate evidence and warrant: separating one paper from the stack and placing it in a sleeve make it less visible. The selection marks importance; the placement may suggest hiding.

3. Diagnose cautiously: Reader B’s response suggests that secrecy may need a stronger cue for this reader. I do not diagnose the reader as wrong or claim that two comments establish a universal failure.

4. Complete revised version: “The courtroom emptied. Inez stacked every paper except the unsigned statement. She waited until the bailiff turned away before folding it into her sleeve.”

5. Explain the mechanism: timing the action to another person looking away connects concealment with avoiding observation. The added beat clarifies behavior without naming the motive.

6. Name the trade-off: the revision makes secrecy less subtle and adds length. It changes both timing detail and sentence structure, so I cannot attribute the whole effect to punctuation alone.

Success check: Ask a fresh reader what Inez appears to keep from view and what remains unknown. A successful response identifies concealment but does not need to agree on fear, guilt, or protection. If no reader is available, describe this as a proposed check, not a completed test.

Compare the Decisions

ExampleEvidence problemDefensible decision
ElevatorWrong grammar label and overly broad speed claim.Correct the label; compare one sentence boundary.
CompassInvented origin and ignored final exchange.Qualify the claim; choose a revision for a stated goal.
CourtroomLimited reader responses could be overgeneralized.Use feedback as a clue; test clearer behavior while preserving motive.

Pause and Try

Which rationale is stronger: “The new version is better because it is dramatic,” or “Waiting for the bailiff to turn away adds a cue of avoiding observation, though it reduces subtlety”?

Pause: say or jot your reasoning before opening the explanation. This is optional, ungraded practice—not a submission.

Check your thinking

The second names a specific change, explains its mechanism, and acknowledges a trade-off. “Dramatic” alone is a reaction, not a warrant.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 6 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Defend a Craft Claim

Purpose and Directions

Apply the lesson skill through evidence-based reasoning, focused original writing, and purposeful revision. Complete every numbered task and submit this work with your vocabulary notes in Notebook Evidence Submission. Quality matters more than length.

Draft for Workshop: “Platform Three”

The departure board blinked from DELAYED to ON TIME. Niko folded the letter into a square small enough to disappear inside his glove. Across the tracks, a woman in a red scarf raised one hand. The train entered the station before he could decide whether she was waving to him.

1. Build the Reasoning Chain

Complete three rows, then write a three-to-four-sentence claim explaining how two choices work together.

ClaimExact evidenceCraft choice and because-reasoning
Record your reasoning in the submission.

2. Choose the Stronger Reasoning

Record A or B, then explain in two or three sentences why your choice makes the stronger evidence-to-effect connection. The answer is not revealed here.

A. The scene is suspenseful because it has a letter, a train, and a mysterious woman.

B. The changing departure board compresses Niko’s decision time, while the letter hidden in his glove withholds its purpose; together these choices make the arriving train interrupt an unresolved choice.

3. Apply the Skill in Your Writing

Write a six-to-eight-sentence scene built around a decision interrupted by an arrival, sound, or deadline. State your intended reader effect and coordinate at least two craft choices. Then add a three-sentence rationale quoting those choices and explaining how they support your goal.

4. Revise and Test the Claim

Revise one sentence that does not fully serve your goal. Show the original and revision, then adjust one sentence of your rationale so the evidence and reasoning match the final draft precisely.

Before You Submit

  • I completed every numbered task.
  • I used exact evidence and explained its effect.
  • I explained my A/B choice.
  • My original writing applies the lesson skill.
  • I made and explained one purposeful revision.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 6 | Page 6 of 6

Checkpoint: Evidence-Based Craft Reasoning

Your Purpose

Independently analyze a new source and apply evidence-based craft reasoning in organized original writing.

Complete all four parts. A score of at least 80% is required.

New Source: “After the Announcement”

The principal’s voice faded from the speaker. Around Tessa, chairs scraped and backpacks zipped. She remained seated, smoothing the same crease in the permission form until the paper began to shine. “You coming?” Malik asked. Tessa folded the form along a different line.

Term support: Craft reasoning connects exact evidence to a named writing choice, its reader effect, and the writer’s purpose.

1. Analyze the Source

  1. Build an evidence-to-effect chain for two exact details: evidence → craft choice → reader effect → possible purpose.
  2. Compare the two folds in the final sentences. Explain how the change functions in the scene without inventing unsupported history.

2. Choose and Defend

Record A or B, then defend your choice in 3–4 sentences using source evidence and a lesson concept. Explain why the other response is weaker.

A. The paper shows Tessa is anxious, so the writer should state the reason for her anxiety immediately.
B. The repeated smoothing and changed fold make the decision visible; the writer could test one additional response if the intended effect needs sharpening.

No answer is revealed before submission. Your choice and reasoning are graded.

3. Create and Organize

Task: Write a 325–425 word scene in which a repeated physical action reveals a character’s changing decision. Follow it with one evidence-based craft paragraph about your own work.

Required organization:

  1. Scene opening—begin with an event that creates pressure and introduce the repeated action.
  2. Scene development—repeat the action with variation while using dialogue or setting to complicate the choice.
  3. Scene turning point and closing—change the action when the character decides, then show the immediate effect.
  4. Craft paragraph—begin with a clear claim, quote one exact detail, name the craft choice, explain the reader effect, and connect it to your purpose.

4. Revise and Explain

Revise either the repeated action or the craft paragraph so the evidence-reasoning chain is complete. Copy both versions and explain the improvement.

Before You Submit

  • Both analysis questions use exact source evidence.
  • Your A/B defense applies the lesson concept and addresses both choices.
  • Your original writing follows the required organization and demonstrates the lesson skill.
  • Your revision is meaningful and your explanation identifies its effect.
  • Your work is original, complete, and carefully proofread.

80% Mastery Requirement

If your score is below 80%, review the identified weakness and follow your TOR’s directions for correction and resubmission.

TOR Help
Contact your Teacher of Record if you need clarification, feedback, or support before submitting your work.
